FRB: Finance and Economics Discussion Series Working Papers en FEDS Paper: The Welfare Effects of Bank Liquidity and Capital Requirements(Revised) Sergio Villalvazo

The stringency of bank liquidity and capital requirements should depend on their social costs and benefits. Equilibrium asset returns yield two simple formulas that express the welfare cost of each requirement as a function of observable variables only. Based on U.S. data, the welfare cost of a 10% liquidity requirement is equivalent to a permanent loss in consumption of about 0.02%, a modest impact. Even using conservative measurements, the cost of a similarly sized increase in the capital requirement is roughly tenfold. Still, optimal policy relies on both requirements to mitigate moral hazard from deposit insurance and is close to Basel III levels.]]> FEDS Paper FEDS Paper: Where's The Bank? Banking Access in the Era of Branch Consolidation(Revised) Robert M. Adams and Shane M. Sherlund

The number of U.S. bank branches fell more than 19 log points between 2014 and 2024, prompting concerns about eroding access to banking services. We study this contraction using a free-entry, two-dimensional spatial competition model in the tradition of Lösch and Hotelling. The model predicts that equilibrium branch density scales linearly with local customer density and that the elasticity of mean nearest-branch distance with respect to the number of branches is -1/2 . Using branch locations and census-block-level data on households and employment, we estimate elasticities between -0.37 and -0.52. These lie near the two-dimensional prediction and reject the -1 implied by one-dimensional models. Differences in branch access across demographic groups are economically small, and they did not widen over the decade. The branch contraction is consistent with the equilibrium response of a competitive spatial system to an industry-wide profitability shock, rather than a localized withdrawal of service.]]> FEDS Paper FEDS Paper: Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence Nick Carollo, Leland D. Crane, Daniel Garcia Molina, and Joseph Nichols

We assess the current evidence on how AI-related investment and the use of AI are affecting the U.S. macroeconomy. Specifically, we document the boom in data center capital investment, the current rate of adoption of AI tools in the economy, the impact of the AI-related investment surge on prices, and discuss whether AI tools have affected the labor market and productivity yet. Driven by current and expected future demand for AI services, investment in data centers, both the physical structures and semiconductor chips and other IT equipment inside the structures, has climbed sharply. AI adoption is growing rapidly both among consumers and firms, though most firms are currently not using AI very intensively or at all. AI model-producing firms have also grown extremely fast, and now account for a noticeable fraction of software industry gross output. Prices have climbed in sectors that provide direct inputs to the data centers, such as memory chips. Effects on the labor market so far appear small and somewhat mixed. Similarly, the effects of AI on aggregate productivity growth also appear to be small so far, and the recent pickup in productivity likely reflects factors that predated the diffusion on generative AI.]]> FEDS Paper FEDS Paper: Costly Misdemeanours: Labour Market Effects of Low-Level Drink-Driving Violations Kabir Dasgupta, Marco Francesconi, Jonathan James, Linda Kirkpatrick, and Alexander Plum

This paper estimates the causal effect of a drink-driving conviction on labour market outcomes. Using linked administrative data and variation in the timing of first convictions in a staggered difference-in-differences design, we compare individuals before and after conviction to those convicted later. We find employment falls by 6–7 percentage points and monthly earnings decline by around 2 percent. The effects are driven primarily by reduced job entry as opposed to job loss. Employment effects are largest in industries where employers are more likely to screen applicants for criminal convictions.]]> FEDS Paper FEDS Paper: Heterogeneity in Service Fee Sensitivity: Evidence from ATM Surcharges Krzysztof Wozniak

Service fees continue to proliferate in a wide range of markets, from retail to payments, generating questions about their impact on consumer choice, competition, and fairness. This paper explores how sensitivity to such fees varies across consumers, use cases, and competitive settings, and whether it is affected by consumer learning. I am able to conduct this in-depth empirical analysis thanks to a uniquely detailed, high-frequency panel data set on surcharged ATM cash withdrawals. Results show that average elasticity estimates mask substantial heterogeneity in consumer sensitivity to service fees. I explore ways in which market and behavioral mechanisms can help explain this heterogeneity. Finally, I investigate whether consumers strategically adjust their behavior in response to service fees.]]> FEDS Paper FEDS Paper: Measuring Consumption with Credit Card Data: Benchmarking and Beyond Aditya Aladangady, Ricardo Duque Gabriel, and Carlo Wix

We introduce a novel monthly county-level consumption dataset constructed from spending data on over 350 million credit cards in the Federal Reserve’s Y-14M reports, covering over 3,000 U.S. counties since 2014. We first show that the data closely track traditional consumption measures, explaining 92 percent of the variation in monthly adjusted personal consumption expenditures (PCE) growth at the national level, capturing meaningful cross-sectional variation in annual adjusted PCE growth at the state level, and reproducing the impulse response of official consumption measures to identified monetary policy shocks. We then use the county-month panel to estimate heterogeneous consumption responses to monetary policy shocks across the county-level income distribution, an analysis infeasible with traditional consumption data. We find suggestive evidence that low-income counties exhibit larger spending declines than high-income counties, consistent with heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian models. Finally, we provide practical guidance for researchers working with similar data, discussing coverage, sample composition, and the approximation of credit card spending from credit bureau data.]]> FEDS Paper FEDS Paper: A Macroeconomic Analysis of Household Labor Supply Responses to Large Fiscal Transfers Isabel Cairó, Shigeru Fujita, and Camilo Morales-Jimenez

The fiscal transfers deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic were unprecedented in scale and strongly progressive. Using CPS/ASEC data, we document that the decline in employment during the pandemic was larger for low-income households and tightly linked to the intensity of transfer receipt, a pattern absent during the Global Financial Crisis. We develop and estimate a two-sector, heterogeneous-household general equilibrium model in which low-income households are borrowing-constrained in normal times but can save out of sufficiently large transfers. Because preferences permit wealth effects on labor supply, transfers both reduce labor supply and raise consumption, and a dollar of transfers is split roughly evenly between the two margins. We find that the effects of transfers are state-dependent: because the borrowing constraint binds more tightly in a deeper recession, the same transfer relaxes a tighter constraint and delivers an employment and consumption response about 40 to 50 percent larger during the pandemic than when the same transfer is introduced in the steady state. In the model, transfers were welfare-improving for recipients, with gains diminishing as transfers increase.]]> FEDS Paper FEDS Paper: Inattentive Price Setting and Inflation Under Fiscal Policy Uncertainty Edson Wu

How do high public debt and fiscal uncertainty interact to shape inflation? We develop a model in which firms face uncertainty about both marginal costs and fiscal policy and choose how much information to acquire before setting prices. Higher debt raises steady-state taxes, affecting attention through two opposing forces. While these taxes reduce the profit stakes of mispricing, they make desired prices more sensitive to tax fluctuations, increasing the value of information. The interaction generates a U-shaped relationship between public debt and attention, and therefore between debt and inflation volatility. Using euro-area firm-level expectations data, we document that the passthrough of expected input-cost growth into expected selling-price growth rises systematically with a country's debt-to-GDP ratio, consistent with the model. In the calibrated general-equilibrium model, an increase in debt from 100% to 175% of GDP raises inflation volatility by about 20%, mainly because firms reallocate attention toward fiscal shocks.]]> FEDS Paper FEDS Paper: Bells and Whistles of Nowcasting Models: Which Matter and When? Manuel González-Astudillo

This paper investigates which features of a Bayesian dynamic factor model improve U.S. GDP nowcasts and whether their contribution varies across historical episodes. Using pseudo-real-time information sets for 25 series, we estimate 16 combinations of dynamic heterogeneity, stochastic volatility, time-varying long-run growth, and a multiplicative outlier adjustment. We evaluate their marginal contributions to point, density, and quantile score forecasts using balanced paired factorial contrasts. Dynamic heterogeneity improves point, density, and tail forecasts, and it is the only feature that helps consistently across all three criteria. Stochastic volatility improves density and tail forecasts in some periods but not point forecasts consistently. Time-varying long-run growth lowers squared-error loss in some periods but worsens tail forecasts. The outlier adjustment does not improve point or density forecasts overall, has favorable but imprecisely estimated effects on upper-tail quantile scores during the pandemic, and worsens those scores afterward.]]> FEDS Paper FEDS Paper: Measuring and Projecting U.S. Investment in Semiconductor Manufacturing Capacity David M. Byrne, Robert Kurtzman, and Heidi L. Williams

We consider official and alternative data sources for measuring and projecting the role of U.S. manufacturing in the global semiconductor manufacturing industry. We find that the government sources we consider face significant limitations for tracking semiconductor fab investment in real time: they use industry and product categories that are too broad, and come with substantial publication lags. We then analyze project-level alternative data from Semiconductor Equipment and Materials International (SEMI), which provides quarterly tracking of individual fab projects with greater timeliness and specificity. Comparing SEMI data with official statistics through 2023, we find broad consistency in investment levels, validating SEMI as a credible supplement to official statistics. This work provides both a practical guide for tracking real-time trends in semiconductor manufacturing and a case study in synthesizing government and alternative data sources.]]> FEDS Paper FEDS Paper: How Did CECL Affect Bank Lending? Ben Ranish and Cindy M. Vojtech

Adoption of the current expected credit losses (CECL) methodology for loan loss provisioning significantly altered how banks recognize loan losses in their capital calculations. Because capital is a more costly funding source for banks, the accounting change affects banks' cost of funding loans. Using variation in the timing and effect of CECL implementation across firms and loan types, this paper finds that loan loss allowances have a similar causal effect on credit supply as capital requirements. Within our sample, the effect of CECL adoption on loan allowances reduced loan growth by approximately 77 basis points annually in the years following adoption. We find no significant effect of CECL on capital distributions.]]> FEDS Paper FEDS Paper: Beyond Financial Conditions: Measuring Structural Vulnerabilities in the U.S. Financial System Michele Modugno, Benjamin Roscoe, Sarah Zoi

We introduce the Financial Vulnerability Index (FVI), a novel indicator of financial vulnerabilities in the U.S. Unlike financial condition indices, which measure current credit market conditions and spike during periods of financial turmoil, the FVI displays the gradual build-up of structural financial weaknesses and declines as such episodes materialize. We demonstrate that the FVI exhibits properties consistent with theoretical mechanisms of financial vulnerabilities. When the index is high, adverse shocks are substantially amplified, generating larger declines in consumption and investment. We provide new empirical evidence that monetary tightening is associated with gradual declines in the FVI, with this effect substantially delayed, taking a few years to fully materialize. Moreover, monetary policy transmission to prices depends on the state of financial vulnerabilities, with significantly stronger effects when vulnerabilities are low.]]> FEDS Paper FEDS Paper: Optimal Pooling in Taylor Rule Estimation with Multiple-Horizon Forecast Panels Edward Herbst and Karen Page

Multiple-horizon forecast panels are increasingly used to infer perceived monetary policy rules, but inference depends on how coefficients are pooled across forecasters, dates, and horizons. We treat this pooling structure as the object of inference. In a participant-date-horizon Taylor-rule regression model, we compare pooling patterns using Bayesian marginal likelihoods, applying the framework to the Blue Chip Financial Forecasts, Survey of Professional Forecasters, and the Summary of Economic Projections. The preferred specifications place much of the systematic variation in policy-rate forecasts in intercepts that vary across forecast horizons and survey dates. Evidence of "changing perceptions" of monetary policy via economically meaningful time-varying response coefficients is weak overall.]]> FEDS Paper FEDS Paper: Premiums or Peril Erik Heitfield, Mallick Hossain, and Katie Merritt

Using fine-grained data on 465,000 Florida home sales over twelve years and semiparametric machine learning methods, we examine how home prices respond to weather-related risk factors. After controlling for geography, home characteristics, and transaction features, we find that home prices are negatively related to property-level expected weather losses derived from catastrophe models, insurance premiums, and exposure to recent hurricanes, but with notably different magnitudes. Expected weather losses show the strongest association with prices and are consistent with markets rationally capitalizing anticipated future losses into current property valuations. Insurance premiums have a statistically significant but economically more modest negative effect on home prices, suggesting that housing market participants may view premium differences across properties as more transitory. Recent hurricane exposure has only a marginal effect on house prices, suggesting that hurricane risk is well-understood in Florida so that realized weather events convey little new information about future losses.]]> FEDS Paper FEDS Paper: The Flight to Affordability: Effects of Pandemic Rent Increases on Renters By Geography Erin Troland, Isabella Agnes, Jessica Liu, Fatimah Shalaan, Michelle Tran, and Douglas Webber

In the pandemic era, people moved from high-density, expensive areas to more affordable areas, putting upward pressure on local housing prices. We examine the geographic distribution of rent growth during this time and its effects on renters. We use administrative new lease data from RealPage and household-level data on rent and income from the American Community Survey. We analyze rents and incomes using Public Use Microdata Areas grouped in two ways: by prepandemic rent levels and by pre-pandemic rent-to-income ratios. Rents grew more in areas with lower pre-pandemic rents but not in areas with lower rent-to-income ratios, consistent with higher-income remote workers moving away from high rent areas to more affordable areas. Lower-income households experienced larger increases in rent relative to their income compared to the median renter. However, area-level rent-to-income ratios reflect both compositional changes in renter populations from mobility and changes in local rents. We highlight the need for future work to track affordability for the same households over time to fully understand pandemic era affordability trends.]]> FEDS Paper
